item.title: Modular Arithmetic
item.description: A timestamp contains more information than most questions about time require. If it is Thursday and we want to know the weekday 365 days later, carrying the year, month, hour, and second through the calculation would be ceremony. We only need $$ (3+365)\bmod 7=4, $$ where Monday is day zero. The large counter has been projected onto a seven-position clock. This projection is not merely a space-saving trick. It gives us an arithmetic system in which values remain bounded while addition and multiplication still behave predictably.

item.title: Binary Exponentiation
item.description: Computing $a^n$ by multiplying by $a$ exactly $n-1$ times is reasonable when $n$ is five. It is less attractive when $n$ is a 64-bit integer or a cryptographic exponent. The exponent contains enough structure to do better. Every time it is even, we can halve it by squaring the base: $$ \begin{aligned} a^{2k} &= (a^k)^2,\ a^{2k+1} &= (a^k)^2a. \end{aligned} $$ This is binary exponentiation, also called exponentiation by squaring. Each step removes one binary digit of $n$, so it uses $O(\log n)$ multiplications.

item.title: Extended Euclidean Algorithm
item.description: The ordinary Euclidean algorithm answers a yes-or-no question about modular division: an integer $a$ has an inverse modulo $m$ exactly when $\gcd(a,m)=1$. The extended algorithm also constructs that inverse. Its output is a triple $(g,x,y)$ satisfying Bézout’s identity: $$ g=\gcd(a,b)=ax+by. $$ When $b=m$ and $g=1$, reducing the identity modulo $m$ erases the second term: $$ ax+my=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad ax\equiv1\pmod m. $$ Thus $x$ is the inverse of $a$ modulo $m$. #Recovering the CoefficientsEuclid’s algorithm repeatedly uses

item.title: Montgomery Multiplication
item.description: Reducing one product modulo $n$ is a division problem. Reducing a thousand products by the same $n$ is a representation problem. Montgomery multiplication changes the representation of every residue so that reduction uses the inexpensive operations modulo a power of two. Entering and leaving the representation has a cost, so the method is useful for chains of products—modular exponentiation is the standard example—not for one isolated %. #Montgomery SpaceChoose a radix $R=2^w$ larger than an odd modulus $n$.

item.title: Finite Fields
item.description: The integers modulo $m$ look almost like ordinary numbers. We can add, subtract, and multiply them, but division is troublesome: modulo $10$, there is no value $x$ for which $2x \equiv 1$. The element $2$ has no multiplicative inverse because it shares a factor with the modulus. When the modulus is prime, this obstruction disappears. Every nonzero residue has an inverse, algebra works the way we expect, and a finite set of integers becomes a field.

item.title: Error Correction
item.description: Copying a bit gives us no protection: if we later read 1, we cannot know whether the original value was 1 or whether a stored 0 was flipped. Copying it three times does. The valid representations are 000 and 111; after one bit flip, the received word is still closer to the correct one. This is the central trade-off of error-correcting codes. We spend extra space or bandwidth to move valid messages farther apart, then use that distance to detect or repair corruption.

item.title: Cryptography
item.description: Cryptography is often introduced as a collection of difficult arithmetic problems. That is a little like introducing aviation as a collection of strong metal alloys: the components matter, but the interesting question is how they are assembled into a system that remains safe when someone is actively trying to break it. An adversary may read traffic, modify it, replay an old message, impersonate one endpoint, or measure how long a computation takes.

item.title: Hashing
item.description: A hash function takes a potentially large object and returns a small fixed-size value. That description sounds suspiciously similar to compression, except that a hash has no decompressor. Information is deliberately discarded, so collisions—different inputs with the same hash—are not an accident but a mathematical certainty. The useful property is that good hash values behave enough like uniformly distributed integers for a particular task. The phrase “enough like” carries most of the complexity.

item.title: Random Number Generation
item.description: Ask a computer for a random bit twice with the same program state and it will normally return the same answer twice. This is not a defect. Most software does not generate new entropy; it expands a small seed into a long deterministic sequence that merely has the statistical shape required by the application. Determinism is valuable for simulations, randomized algorithms, tests, and games. A failing run can be replayed from its seed, and generating each value costs only a few arithmetic instructions.
